title: The real question we should all be asking about AI
content: The stock market is turning its back on Big Tech. Google just had its worst day ever. Intel tumbled more than any day since the Nixon administration. Amazon and Meta both had significant declines this week, too. The Nasdaq tumbled and is just over a percentage point away from a correction (a 10% decline from its all-time high). The common thread: Building the infrastructure to power AI is really, really expensive – and Big Tech profits aren’t yet justifying that massive expense. AI companies are increasingly doling out more cash for data centers than their businesses are able to generate. But if the stock market is supposed be to delivering some kind of message, Big Tech isn’t hearing it. Spending on AI has reached $1.6 trillion since 2023 and is expected to hit $1 trillion every single year for the next decade or so, according to JPMorgan. None of that changed this week. That’s because the market that’s financing all of this – the bond market – is mostly shrugging its shoulders while the stock market is in the midst of a mild freakout. Lenders have been lining up to take on Big Tech’s debt to pay for the technology that’s reshaping the global economy. That means the questions the market seems to be asking about AI – will Big Tech keep growing its spending? (it most certainly will) and will AI will turn a profit anytime soon? (doesn’t look like it) – are the wrong ones. The real question we should be asking about AI is: How much longer will the bond market sustain the nonstop spending spree? That will ultimately dictate whether AI turns into a success or a bust. The way AI math works is like this: Spend a lot of money upfront on the infrastructure needed to support AI (data centers, servers, chips, power, labor, building materials, etc.). Then, once the data center is switched on, AI companies can monetize that investment … somewhere between three months to two years later, according to Goldman Sachs. With profit arriving that far down the road, hyperscalers (the Big Tech guys like Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta) need to borrow a ton of money upfront and pay back investors down the road. “A ton” doesn’t really do it justice. Those four hyperscalers alone have been collectively responsible for more than a third of all capital expenditures from the S&P 500 over the past 12 months, notes John Higgins, chief economic adviser at Capital Economics. That’s why a third of Big Tech’s capital expenditures this year are expected to be financed with debt – something like $250 billion worth of bonds from hyperscalers alone, according to Goldman Sachs. That’s expected to peak next year at around 35% of hyperscalers’ spending. But bond market investors don’t have infinite money to spend. And there’s a ton of competition for lending right now – especially from US Treasuries as the government is trying to pay for Social Security, Medicare and an expensive war, all at the same time. That raises an obvious question: Exactly how much money are investors willing to lend AI companies? It’s more than you might think. The hypothetical maximum amount of debt the market can absorb is unknowable, but Goldman Sachs did the math anyway and came up with $510 billion of available investment-grade (top-tier) debt for the biggest hyperscalers. That’s more than double what they’re currently expected to be borrowing by the end of the year. In other words: The biggest AI companies have a lot of runway left to borrow. The question isn’t how much; the question is how much longer . The answer depends on two parts: Who is paying and who is receiving. “We are not concerned about access to capital,” said Amanda Lynam, chief credit strategist for Goldman Sachs on a recent company podcast . “We are just expecting there to be a more nuanced conversation about where to issue and at what price.” Private investment funds, venture funds and private equity are ready to do the heavy lifting to support the AI buildout, Lynam said, with trillions more dollars of “dry powder” to finance it. But hyperscalers aren’t the only game in town. Other companies, including neoclouds, are playing in the space too. They’re highly indebted companies that rent out computing to other businesses, and their credit situation is starting to look iffy. Their non-investment-grade bonds deliver high yields that investors willing to take on more risk are willing to gamble on, in exchange for potentially massive rewards.. That’s the market in which CoreWeave plays, with its bond yields surging to 15% this month as losses piled up. Elon Musk said the neocloud industry, which includes CoreWeave, is due for a massive shakeout (he called it “guppy-level death.”) Every new technology has winners and losers, and Musk may be right about neoclouds. We’ll see. Hyperscalers, by contrast, look like winners. Their cloud revenue (a stat Wall Street uses to measure AI demand) grew 50% in the second quarter. They have huge contract backlogs and the capacity to absorb higher borrowing costs. Those bottlenecks can support high prices, which helped hyperscaler revenue surge 19% over the past 12 months, according to Higgins. And the advent of agentic AI has sent demand exploding: requests from agents consume 15 times as many tokens as human-initiated requests, according to OpenRouter. “The outlook for these things doesn’t look obviously bleak, given that AI is gradually being used more and more in the economy,” Higgins said. The concern is that the cost of borrowing could get unwieldy. And that could change the economics that are still working for AI. Negative sentiment that’s pervasive in the stock market could start to bleed out into the bond market, sending bond yields higher and raising borrowing costs for AI companies. The bond market works best when there’s an end in sight, Lyman noted. Every AI investor believes there’s a light at the end of the tunnel. We just have no idea how long this tunnel is. The uncertainty about when companies will ultimately start turning a profit and making money off all their massive AI investments could give the bond market pause, she said. In the meantime, the outlook for the technology and the big companies’ finances looks quite strong, said Stephanie Aliaga, a global market strategist with JPMorgan, in a recent note to investors. Warning signs would include a downshift in businesses’ AI usage, cheaper pricing or fewer customer commitments. We’re not seeing any of those yet.

title: Soaring cost of Halloween treats spooks shoppers
content: Halloween shoppers in the US seeking sweet relief this spooky season have instead been shocked by the high price of seasonal treats, as cost of living pressures continue to bite. Demetrio Beltres, a 33-year-old financial adviser searching for Halloween bargains for trick or treaters said he was spending more than his usual $15 (£11) to $20 this year because prices were much higher. "I'm trying to spend at least $20 to $30 just to make sure that I get the kids something," he said, while browsing the rows of colour options at a Target in Manhattan. A lot of people are finding they are in the same boat as Demetrio this year. Stephen Zagor, adjunct associate professor at Columbia Business School, said people have only so much to spend, and when everyday essentials are costing more, people may feel less inclined to make this the most extravagant Halloween. "I think the holiday's gotten scary, more from an economic [perspective], than it might be for scaring people at the door," he said. Analysis from left-leaning non-profit Groundwork Collaborative and the Century Foundation found the cost of popular Halloween chocolates and confectionery was 15.3% higher this year than in 2025. Separate research from personal finance firm Finance Buzz found prices for Halloween treats have soared by 71% over the past five years - a much bigger increase than the general pace of price rises over the same period. The price of confectionery generally has been pushed up thanks to higher cocoa prices. The cost of a tonne of cocoa skyrocketed to a high of more than $10,700 in January 2025, according to figures from the International Monetary Fund via the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis, as climate change contributed to severe weather which affected supplies. "The cocoa that is now being consumed was bought when the prices were high," said Zagor, who specialises in food businesses. Cost of living pressures have also increased, with inflation running at 3.7%, and fuel prices remain high. Diesel, at $6.32 a gallon, is only 20 cents below the record reached in September. People shopping for Halloween treats in New York were noticing the price pressures. "Everything is expensive, so it does not surprise me that Halloween candy is expensive too," said Mallory, who declined to give her last name. The combined cost of living pressures have affected how much people are buying in the run up to the holiday, according to consumer and market research company Nielsen IQ. It found Halloween treat sales were down 11.7% by the middle of September, and by the middle of October sales were down 6.7%. Chris Costagli, NielsenIQ's vice-president of US food thought leadership, said shoppers appeared more willing to spend as Halloween neared, but remained cautious. "Sales have improved considerably from where we started in September, with smaller packs gaining ground while larger sizes continue to struggle," he said. "This feels like a consumer who still wants the occasion, but is paying much closer attention to what goes into the basket." Zagor, who is a fan of Halloween as well as traditional Halloween treats, said cutting back on costs, could present a good opportunity to offer trick or treaters a different kind of experience when they come to your door. "It could be how you present the candy when kids come to your house as much as the one piece of candy that you're going to give," he said. Options could include using a spooky fake skeleton hand to share out treats, rather than letting children reach into a bowl, or dressing up to meet trick or treaters. Zagor said making your own treats is another option, inviting people over to make them together. "You could certainly do something slightly magical, slightly interesting," he suggested. "The trick literally could be as important as the treat."
ranking_reason: The cost of Halloween treats has increased by 15.3% this year, affecting how much people are willing to spend on the holiday. The article provides substantive information on the economic impact of this development.

title: Hackers just stole $6 billion in crypto. It’s not the first time, and it won’t be the last
content: For years, the crypto industry has tried to shed its affiliation with crime while marketing itself as a safe alternative to traditional banking and investing. But once again, a record-shattering heist is deepening concerns about crypto’s vulnerabilities. On Thursday, the world’s biggest crypto exchange, Binance, saw more than $6 billion siphoned from its system in the span of about 20 minutes. About half of those funds were linked to a kind of cryptocurrency known as stablecoins, which were quickly frozen by the firms that issue them. The other funds were tied up in digital tokens such as bitcoin and ether, which don’t have centralized governing authorities and are likely impossible to recover, according to crypto researchers. Binance’s losses could top $3 billion, according to researchers. While that is a small fraction of the exchange’s $155 billion in total user assets, it eclipses the $1 billion emergency fund Binance had set aside for situations like this. The company pledged to cover the losses with those emergency reserves and other assets, emphasizing that “user funds are safe.” Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals Thursday, just hours after a smaller security breach throttled operations at Polymarket, the crypto-powered prediction market. This was the second apparent hack of Polymarket since June and was likely unrelated to the Binance incident. Some 700 Polymarket users lost $2.7 million in unauthorized withdrawals, according to analytics firm Bubblemaps . Like Binance, Polymarket promised to make customers whole. But security experts warn that covering customer losses isn’t much of a long-term strategy. “The fact that Binance may have the balance sheet to absorb the damage is encouraging, but I wouldn’t confuse financial strength with operational security,” Ryan Kirkley, CEO of crypto infrastructure firm Global Settlement Network, said in an email. “We’re talking about the world’s largest crypto exchange relying on emergency freezes and reimbursement promises,” he said. “That’s a serious problem for an industry asking institutions to trust it with substantially more capital.” To be sure, any business can be vulnerable to a cyberattack. But centralized exchanges like Binance have become high-value targets for hackers, in part because they exist outside the strict regulations that banks and other financial institutions must adhere to. And crypto has long been favored by criminal enterprises because it can move funds quickly and anonymously across borders. Binance, which was founded in China but lacks a fixed headquarters, pleaded guilty in 2023 to violating US federal anti-money-laundering rules, among other charges — a case that landed its Canadian founder, Changpeng Zhao, in prison for four months. Zhao was pardoned by President Donald Trump last year but remains legally prohibited from running Binance. AI is turbocharging security risks across the internet. In Thursday’s Binance hack, researchers at Chainalysis said they observed “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that “thousands of transactions in a short period suggest that the attackers are using automation to obscure the trail of funds .” And despite a warm embrace from the Trump administration, crypto remains a risky business with few regulations on the books. In the United States, the vast majority of people investing in crypto do so through centralized exchanges that lack the kind of federal deposit insurance provided by traditional banks. “Centralized exchanges pose a risk because they’re centralized… once that system gets hacked, everybody’s funds can be compromised,” said Iman Shafiei, founder of Keystone Research Group, in an email. The simplest protection, he said, is to not leave funds sitting on the same exchanges where you buy and sell. “The moment you want to hold, move your crypto to a self-custody wallet.” Of course, self-custody, in which a person manages their own digital wallet, comes with its own potential headaches. If an account holder loses their password, there is no customer service hotline to call and those funds are effectively gone. In 2021, Chainalysis estimated that around 20% of all the bitcoin ever created may be lost or stranded in wallets that account holders can no longer access.
